- When sentiment shows strong positive momentum (e.g., >0.67) followed by a sharp drop, model tends to over-forecast and overshoots; reduce forecast peak by 5–10%.
- If sentiment turns negative (e.g., <0.33) after a recent spike, model often fails to adjust downward; apply a downward bias of 3–8% based on sentiment magnitude.
- Model consistently overestimates prices during high-news-volume periods (news=3.0) unless sentiment is strongly negative — reduce forecast by 2–5% if sentiment is neutral or weak.
- After a strong upward sentiment spike (e.g., sentiment >0.8), model often overreacts and forecasts too high; apply a 5–10% correction to peak values.
- If sentiment change is negative and recent (last 3–5 days), model tends to lag — adjust forecast downward by 2–5% to align with sentiment decay.
- Mean reversion is evident when model forecasts stay above 75% of historical range; cap forecasts at 75% of 30-day moving average if sentiment is weak or neutral.
- Overshoots after sentiment spikes are common — if model forecast > 75% of 30-day high, reduce by 5–10% unless sentiment remains strong.
- If sentiment is consistently low (e.g., <0.33) over 3+ days, model often underestimates — increase forecast by 2–5% to account for potential rebound.
